lessons.title: First-year balance, principal, and interest on a mortgage
lessons.intro: You take out a $120,000 mortgage at 6.125% APR, paid monthly over 30 years. The first payment lands in April, so your first calendar year contains only payments 1 through 9. How much do you still owe at year end, and how much of what you paid actually reduced the debt?

steps.explain: Reset the calculator so nothing left over from earlier work leaks into this problem. Every variable returns to its default and the display shows 0.00.
This loan is paid monthly, so tell the calculator there are 12 payments in a year. Entering P/Y also sets the compounding periods C/Y to 12 automatically.
Leave the settings screen and return to the calculator's standard display.
The loan runs 30 years. The xP/Y shortcut multiplies 30 by the 12 payments per year, so N becomes 360 monthly payments without you doing the arithmetic.
Store the annual rate. The screen rounds it to 6.13, but the calculator keeps the full 6.125 internally — never re-type the rounded number you see.
Store the loan amount as a positive present value: it is money the lender hands to you, so it flows in.
Compute the monthly payment. It comes out negative because it is money you pay out each month.
Open the Amortization worksheet. It greets you with P1, the first payment of the range you want to analyze; after a reset it starts at 1.
Confirm the range starts at payment 1 — the first payment you will actually make.
Move down to P2 and end the range at payment 9. Since the loan started in April, payments 1 through 9 are all that fall in the first calendar year.

Step down to BAL: the loan balance remaining right after payment 9. The schedule works from the payment rounded to two decimals, -729.13, which is why this can differ by a cent or two from a future-value calculation.
Step down to PRN: the principal repaid across payments 1-9. It is negative because paying down principal is money out of your pocket.
Step down to INT: the interest paid across payments 1-9, also negative as an outflow. Notice interest dwarfs principal this early in the loan.

lessons.answer: After nine payments you still owe $118,928.63. Of the $6,562.17 you paid, only $1,071.37 reduced the debt (PRN = -1,071.37) while $5,490.80 went to interest (INT = -5,490.80) — both negative because they are money you paid out.

lessons.title: Moving the schedule to the next year
lessons.intro: Same $120,000 mortgage at 6.125% over 30 years. The second calendar year covers payments 10 through 21 — a full twelve months this time. You will read that year's figures, then let the calculator slide the window to year three for you with a single key.

steps.explain: Start from a clean slate so this lesson stands on its own.
Set 12 payments per year for the monthly mortgage, then leave the settings screen.
Enter the term: 30 years times 12 payments gives N = 360.
Store the 6.125% annual rate; the display rounds to 6.13 but the exact value is kept.
Store the amount borrowed as a positive inflow.
Compute the monthly payment again: -729.13, negative because you pay it.
Open the Amortization worksheet and start the range at payment 10, the first payment of the second calendar year.
End the range at payment 21. Payments 10 through 21 are the twelve payments of year two.
Read BAL: what you still owe right after payment 21.

Read PRN: principal repaid during year two. It beats year one's 1,071.37 for two reasons: year two holds twelve payments to year one's nine, and each month a little more of your payment chips away at the debt.
Read INT: interest paid during year two, still the lion's share of the 12 x 729.13 you handed over.
One more press past INT wraps the worksheet back around to P1, still showing the old starting payment.
With P1 on screen, CPT slides the whole window forward by its own width: 10-21 becomes 22-33, the third year, with no typing.
Check P2: it moved too, landing on 33. You could still overwrite it if you wanted a different range.
Read year three's ending balance after payment 33.
Year three's principal: the payoff keeps accelerating.
Year three's interest: slightly less than year two's, because the balance it is charged on keeps shrinking.

lessons.answer: Year two (payments 10-21): BAL = 117,421.60, PRN = -1,507.03, INT = -7,242.53. Pressing CPT on P1 then advances the window to payments 22-33, where BAL = 115,819.62, PRN = -1,601.98, INT = -7,147.58 — each year a bit more principal, a bit less interest.

lessons.title: Sizing a balloon payment after five years
lessons.intro: You sell a property and finance $82,000 for the buyer at 7% annual interest, with monthly payments computed over a 30-year amortization — but the full remaining balance is due as a balloon payment after 5 years. How big is the monthly payment, and how big is the balloon?

steps.explain: Reset so old values cannot contaminate the new loan.
Payments are monthly, so set 12 payments per year and quit the settings screen.
The payment is sized as if the loan ran a full 30 years: N = 360 months. The balloon cuts it short later, but the payment math uses the long schedule.
Store the 7% annual interest rate.
Store the amount financed as a positive present value — from the buyer's side it is money received.
Compute the monthly payment: -545.55, negative because the buyer pays it out each month.
Open the Amortization worksheet. P1 is already 1 from the reset, which is exactly where the range should start.
Move to P2 and use the xP/Y shortcut right inside the worksheet: 5 years times 12 payments makes P2 = 60, the last payment before the balloon comes due.
Read BAL: the balance still owed after payment 60. This is the balloon payment.
Read PRN: in five years of payments the buyer has retired only $4,812.28 of principal — a 30-year schedule barely dents the debt early on.
Read INT: $27,920.72 of the $32,733 paid over five years was interest — which, as the seller, is your earnings on the financing.

lessons.answer: PMT = -545.55 and BAL = 77,187.72 — the buyer pays $545.55 a month for five years, then owes a balloon payment of $77,187.72 after payment 60, having paid $27,920.72 in interest along the way.
